questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) What is 2's complement? Why do modern computers use 2's complement? (2 marks)

(b) Represent the decimal numbers 127 and -128 in 8-bit 2's complement. (4 marks)

(c) Add 127 and -128 in 8-bit 2's complement. What is the denary equivalent of the result obtained? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) 2's complement (2 marks)**

2's complement is a way of representing **signed** integers in binary. A positive number is written as ordinary binary with a leading 0; a negative number is obtained by writing the binary of its magnitude, inverting every bit (1's complement) and adding 1. In an $n$-bit word the leftmost bit has the weight $-2^{n-1}$, so the range is $-2^{n-1}$ to $2^{n-1}-1$ (for 8 bits: $-128$ to $+127$).

Modern computers use it because:

- there is only **one representation of zero** (sign-and-magnitude and 1's complement have both +0 and -0);
- **addition and subtraction use the same adder circuit**: $a - b$ is computed as $a + (-b)$, so no separate subtractor is needed and the sign bit is treated like any other bit; this makes the hardware simpler and cheaper;
- every bit pattern is used and overflow is easy to detect.

**(b) Representation of 127 and -128 on 8 bits (4 marks)**

*127:* $127 = 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1$, so $127 = 01111111_2$ (positive, leading bit 0).

*-128:* the magnitude 128 is $10000000_2$. Invert all bits: $01111111$; add 1: $01111111 + 1 = 10000000$. So $-128 = 10000000_2$ (this is the smallest number that fits in 8 bits).

**(c) Addition of 127 and -128 (3 marks)**

```text
   01111111   (+127)
 + 10000000   (-128)
 ----------
   11111111
```

No carry goes out of the leftmost bit, so there is no overflow. The result $11111111$ starts with 1, so it is negative. To read it: invert, $00000000$, add 1, $00000001 = 1$, hence the value is $-1$. The denary equivalent of the result is **-1**, which is correct since $127 + (-128) = -1$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A RAM has a capacity of 32k×16.

(a) How many memory addresses does this RAM have? (2 marks)

(b) How many address lines will be needed for this RAM? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The notation $32k \times 16$ means 32k words (locations) of 16 bits each, with $1k = 2^{10} = 1024$.

**(a) Number of addresses (2 marks).** $32k = 32 \times 1024 = 32\,768 = 2^{15}$ memory addresses (locations). (The total capacity is $32\,768 \times 16 = 524\,288$ bits, that is 64 KiB.)

**(b) Address lines (2 marks).** $n$ address lines can select $2^n$ locations. We need $2^n \ge 32\,768 = 2^{15}$, so $n = 15$ **address lines** (A0 to A14). (The 16 bits of a word are carried by 16 data lines, which are not asked for.)

questions.enonce_markdown: (iii) State TWO main differences between RISC and CISC machines. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) and CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) differ mainly in the following ways (any two, with an explanation, 2 marks each):

| Feature | RISC | CISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction set | Small set of simple instructions | Large set of complex, powerful instructions (one instruction may do a whole job, e.g. a string move) |
| Instruction length and execution | Fixed length; most instructions execute in **one clock cycle**, which makes pipelining easy | Variable length; instructions take several clock cycles |
| Memory access | Only LOAD and STORE instructions access memory; other operations work on registers | Many instructions can work directly on memory operands |
| Registers | Many general-purpose registers | Fewer registers |
| Control unit | Hard-wired (fast, simple) | Micro-programmed (microcode) |
| Programs and compilers | Longer programs (more instructions), more work for the compiler | Shorter programs, simpler compiler, less memory for code |

Example answer: *"A RISC processor has a small set of simple instructions, whereas a CISC processor has a large set of complex instructions. In a RISC processor most instructions are executed in one clock cycle, whereas CISC instructions need several cycles."*
